title: The Rutli Oath and the Swiss Alliance
text:
In early August 1291, the men of three valley communities around Lake Lucerne, Uri, Schwyz and Nidwalden, drew up a charter in Latin. They promised to help one another with all their power, inside and outside their valleys, against anyone who attacked them. They also agreed not to accept any judge who had bought his office or who was not a native of their valleys, and set rules for settling disputes among themselves. The document, known as the Federal Charter of 1291, survives in an archive in Schwyz.

Around this sober document a famous legend grew up. Written down in the fifteenth century in the White Book of Sarnen, and later polished by the chronicler Aegidius Tschudi, it tells of three men, Walter Furst of Uri, Werner Stauffacher of Schwyz and Arnold of Melchtal from Unterwalden, who met secretly on the Rutli, a meadow above the lake, and swore an oath to free their valleys from harsh Habsburg bailiffs. The same tradition includes the tale of William Tell.

The alliance itself was real and lasting. In 1315 the confederates defeated a Habsburg army at Morgarten, and in the following centuries other towns and valleys joined, until the confederation grew into modern Switzerland.

In the nineteenth century the Swiss adopted 1 August as their national day, and the Rutli meadow remains a national symbol, visited every year by people from across the country.
lesson: Small communities that pledge to defend one another can stand up to far greater powers. A clear written promise outlasts the heroes of the story.
people: Uri, Schwyz, Nidwalden (Unterwalden); legendary figures Walter Furst, Werner Stauffacher, Arnold of Melchtal
source: Federal Charter of 1291 (Bundesbrief), Schwyz; White Book of Sarnen (c. 1470); Aegidius Tschudi, Chronicon Helveticum
caveat: The charter is authentic, but the Rutli oath scene and its three heroes are later legend.
